historical_record.description: The Mutual Amusement and Investment Company built a one-story building, about 60 by 119 feet, holding a nickelodeon movie theater and a store, at a cost of $12,000; it had no backstage, being made only for showing films.
The Sanborn map showed the building with small stores on either side of a moving-picture hall, numbered 2251, 2253 (the theater) and 2255 Fillmore.
A building permit was issued for the theater and its flanking stores, the first building on the lot since the 1906 earthquake and fire; the permit was filed under 2257–59 Fillmore.
The theater was running as the Regent by December 1913, when it showed Mary Pickford in In the Bishop's Carriage.
Operation of the Regent passed from J.P. Hughes to Leroy Blanchard and L.F. Salbach.
G. M. McDonald was the Regent's proprietor.
The Regent appeared in the city directory for the first time, at 2251 Fillmore Street.
An advertisement described the Regent as fully equipped for talking pictures.

Film distributor and exhibitor Herbert Rosener took over the theater to run it under a new name, the Clay-International, as a house for foreign-made films, the first dedicated foreign film theater in San Francisco.
The Clay-International opened with the Swedish musical Sangan till Henne, shown with English titles, followed by French, Spanish, Russian and British films.
New projection equipment, carpet and seats were installed.
The theater began weekly Saturday midnight showings of second-run foreign films, which were dropped after several months.
The theater's name changed from the Clay-International to the Clay Theater, still with a foreign-film program.
Ownership passed from an older ownership group to a group that included the theater operators Richard J. and Henry W. Nasser of Nasser Brothers, builders of the Castro and Alhambra theaters.

A permit was issued for a remodel by theater architect Vincent G. Raney for Nasser Brothers: the vestibule was cut to half its depth to fit a second-floor office, a rounded ticket booth was placed at its south wall, and the arched opening in the façade was filled with a band of casement windows.
A permit was issued to mount neon-lit block letters spelling C-L-A-Y on the canopy.
A fire did $7,000 of damage and closed the theater for four weeks; it reopened with a French film of Dostoyevsky's The Idiot.
The theater joined the San Francisco Museum of Art to preview the art-history documentary Pictura: An Adventure in Art.
The property was sold to Bay Properties, Inc.
CinemaScope and wide-screen projection were installed.

A $15,000 remodel designed by Gale Santocono was permitted: the 1946 vestibule gave way to a metal-and-glass storefront nearer the sidewalk, the small south storefront and the projecting cornice were removed, restrooms replaced the old stairs, and the auditorium seating was rearranged.
Permits were issued to Wonderlite Neon Co. to move the vertical projecting sign and add a double-faced horizontal sign.
Photographed, showing the Clay Theater.
The property was sold to a new ownership group; foreign and prestige films stayed on the program.
Advertising called the theater the New Clay.
The theater held retrospective film festivals for Greta Garbo and Mae West.
The Clay was among the San Francisco theaters giving George Romero's Night of the Living Dead a midnight-only run.
The theater closed for about a year for renovations.

The theater reopened under the direction of Mel Novikoff, operator of the Surf Theater and film curator at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, who added series on fascism, psychiatry and women's cinema to the foreign-film program.
John Waters' Pink Flamingos began a four-month run of midnight showings, ending on November 9, 1974; the theater was not, as sometimes claimed, the site of its first midnight screening.
The theater gave the West Coast premiere of Robert Mapplethorpe's short film Still Moving/Patti Smith, on a bill with videos by the Dead Kennedys, Devo and the Mutants.
Operation of the Surf Theater Group's houses, the Clay among them with the Castro and the Lumiere, passed to Blumfield Enterprises.
A restructuring sale left the property with the same ownership group.
Landmark Theatres took over operation of the theater.
The property was sold.
The theater closed, ending more than a century as a single-screen movie house.
The Board of Supervisors initiated landmark designation of the theater.
The Mayor approved the Board of Supervisors' resolution initiating the theater's landmark designation.
The Historic Preservation Commission recommended the theater's designation as a city landmark.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 302, Clay Theatre.

notable_residents.name: Herbert Rosener
notable_residents.detail: Herbert Rosener, the leading West Coast exhibitor and distributor of art films, ran the theater from 1935 until his death in May 1968.

notable_residents.name: Mel Novikoff
notable_residents.detail: Mel Novikoff, one of San Francisco's most influential programmers of foreign and independent film, ran the theater from its 1973 reopening until his death in 1987.
